prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow optical clocks to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for B040, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Round 1 did not change my view of the science, which I reached on instrument grounds; it showed that members from atomic physics, condensed matter, statistical physics, electron microscopy and theory give the same reasons. The central point is the magic-wavelength condition. It removes the conflict between holding many neutral atoms tightly enough to suppress motional effects and leaving the clock transition unperturbed by the trap light, and that is what let a many-atom signal and an accuracy near 1e-18 coexist. The result has been reproduced and intercompared across independent laboratories, so it does not rest on one group's claim. The two-name credit follows roles that can be described honestly: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks, Ye for taking the platform to the accuracy and stability frontier. On the chair's question about the citation, I would keep it species-neutral, as Kroll suggests, and name the magic-wavelength lattice so that the sentence itself carries the distinction from the comb and ion-clock prizes. I would not cite the redefinition of the second or geodesy, because those are applications that have not yet happened or are still developing.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still distinctness. Hall and Haensch shared the 2005 prize for the comb that every optical clock needs, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, including the ion-clock route. If the committee reads the lattice clock as a third award in one precision-spectroscopy lineage, the pair is weaker than it looks. My answer is that the comb is the readout tool and 2012 concerned single ions; the lattice clock changes the operating principle by interrogating a large neutral ensemble free of trap shifts. I accept that this is a judgement, not a proof. Second, two names leave out Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the supplied evidence does not settle the relative weight of Katori's concept and Ye's accuracy work. Third, part of the broader impact is prospective. Finally, the convergence on B040 is partly the product of members moving after reading each other, so I treat the support count as a prompt to re-test the argument, not as evidence for it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B018, the IceCube diffuse flux with Halzen and Karle, as a new observational channel and a compact two-name credit, lists B040 first among his alternatives, and says he would not object strongly to it. He also says the distinctness of B040 needs more argument.
responses.response: I take his case for B018 seriously and I still keep it as my first alternative. A diffuse TeV-PeV flux well above atmospheric expectations, confirmed in several channels, is a real discovery, and the two-name credit is simpler than for B035 or B023. Where I differ is on timing and on what the citation could say. The dominant sources are unidentified and the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane associations are statistically limited, so the citation would be a measured flux rather than an interpreted result. Leaving out AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND would also need explicit acknowledgement, and I am in the detector world and should be careful not to let that sympathy move me. On his distinctness question about B040, I would put the answer in the citation: neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength, which neither the 2005 nor the 2012 citation describes. If he can accept that sentence, his stated willingness to live with B040 would let the committee vote without a split on merit.

responses.point: Kroll supports B040 with a citation that is species-neutral and speaks of the lattice clock concept. He lists the continuity reading with the 2005 and 2012 prizes among his own case against, and he discloses his stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder.
responses.response: I agree on the species-neutral wording; naming strontium would invite a priority argument with ytterbium that the evidence does not need. I also agree that the distinctness question is the real test, and I would put the distinction in one clause, magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, so the citation answers it. On his disclosure, I do not see a basis for recusal on what he has documented: Hall's role in the 2005 prize bounds B040 but is not a tie to Katori or Ye. Having him in the room is useful, since he is the member best placed to say whether the comb-to-lattice step is a new principle. I would only ask that he state, on the record, whether the Boulder stay gives him any reason to treat Ye differently from Katori.

responses.point: Lindroth separates the 2005 citation, a spectroscopic tool, from a new kind of clock with a different operating principle, and asks whether independent 1e-18 comparisons suffice without the redefinition of the second. She also describes the Katori and Ye roles as conceptual originator and the person who drove it to its limit.
responses.response: I accept her answer on distinctness and I would adopt it nearly verbatim in the citation discussion. On maturity, I think the independent 1e-18 comparisons are sufficient, because the invention and its performance do not depend on the metrology bodies' timetable; the redefinition would only reflect the same result. I would add one limit to her role split. Dividing the citation into originator and record-setter is fair as a description but is not settled by the supplied evidence, so I would not write the roles into the citation and would keep the sentence about the invention and its development. I also agree with her that B018 should be called a serious contender and not dismissed on merit.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B040 for its precisely stated principle, says the citation must rest on the demonstrated invention and not on the redefinition of the second or geodesy, and asks how a pair could be defended for a collaboration of hundreds if B018 were chosen.
responses.response: Her point about not resting on prospective impact is one I now share more firmly than in round 1; I would leave the redefinition out of the citation entirely. On B018, her question about a pair for hundreds of authors is fair, and I have no better answer than that the diffuse-flux case is simple to credit with Halzen as conceiver and Karle in construction and operation. It still leaves the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers unrecognised, which is why I keep B018 as an alternative and not my preference. I also note her disclosure of closeness to B046; since she has set it aside for the reasons she gives, I see no issue.

responses.point: Johansson says the redefinition of the second is an application and not a doubt about the discovery, that the two-name credit is not distorted by a large collaboration, and that she should recuse herself from deliberation and vote on B055 and possibly related superconducting-circuit material. She also ranks IceCube seventh and calls it a strong candidate for a few years from now.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition does not bear on whether the discovery was made, and I welcome her description of the credit. In round 1 I asked for her case that circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 prize; she has since moved to B040, so the question is moot for this vote, but her recusal on B055 should be minuted in case the committee returns to it. On B018, I accept her judgement that it may be stronger after a few more years of source work; I would not want the committee to treat that as a rejection of the achievement. We disagree about the clock mainly in emphasis: I think the diffuse-flux result is established as a flux, and my reservation is about interpretation and credit, not quality.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems; I treat it as distinct but this is a judgement and Danielsson has not yet said he accepts it.

Whether two names suffice given Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups; the supplied evidence offers no case for a third name that I find stronger than the case for the pair.
How the citation should word the division between Katori's concept and first realisation and Ye's accuracy work without stating a priority claim the evidence does not support.

Whether B018 would be mature enough in a later year, once source identification is firmer and independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal develops, and whether my own instrument-builder sympathy affects how I weigh it.
Whether round 1 convergence reflects independent judgement or mutual influence; seven files on one pair is evidence only to the extent the reasons hold up.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to the optical-clock community or to Katori or Ye. My documented PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur work and my CERN doctoral background touch the field of B018 and the detector collaborations in B035. I know of no specific link to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS, and I would flag the proximity and invite scrutiny if either became the leading option. I do not see a reason to recuse Kroll on B040 from his disclosure, but I leave that to the committee.
